subject: economics
title: Trade, choice and scale — Arden
stem:
All places and values are fictional. In Arden, a small domestic market opens to imported tools and gains access to overseas customers for its own manufactured products.

Answer parts (a)–(c) using the initial scenario. For part (d) only, consider the following additional evidence, which may change an initial assumption.

Additional application evidence: Imported machines require skills that domestic workers lack.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain one benefit of imported tools for domestic producers.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how access to overseas customers can lower average production costs.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why consumers and all domestic producers need not benefit equally.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how the additional evidence changes or qualifies the economic interpretation in this case.

steps.text: Access to a wider range of suitable capital equipment can improve productivity.
Firms may produce more or higher-quality output from given resources.
A larger market can support greater output.
Fixed costs may be spread across more units and specialization may become viable.
Economies of scale can reduce average costs, although they are not guaranteed at every scale.
Consumers may gain lower prices and greater variety.
Domestic import-competing firms may lose sales and employment.
Gains from trade can coexist with adjustment costs and unequal distribution of benefits.
Identify the economic determinant, constraint or model assumption affected by this evidence, distinguishing it from the conditions used in the initial analysis.
Technology access does not guarantee productivity gains without complementary human capital. A justified causal link is required for this explanation mark.

subject: economics
title: Comparative advantage from output data — Doreva
stem:
All places and values are fictional. In Doreva, two economies can use the same full-employment resource allocation to make either the maximum food or maximum textiles below. Assume constant opportunity costs.

| Economy | Food units | Textile units |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Home | 60 | 30 |
| Partner | 40 | 40 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate each economy's opportunity cost of one textile unit.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify comparative advantage in each good.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State a mutually beneficial terms-of-trade range for one textile and explain.

steps.text: 2 food units.
Partner:40/40.
1 food unit.
Partner has comparative advantage in textiles because its food opportunity cost is lower.
Home has comparative advantage in food:0.50 textile per food versus 1 for Partner.
Strictly between 1 and 2 food units per textile for strict gains to both.
Partner receives more food than its 1-food opportunity cost.
Home gives less food than its 2-food domestic cost of producing textiles; endpoints give one side no strict gain.

title: A tariff in a small open economy — Gavela
subtopic: A tariff in a small open economy
stem:
All places and values are fictional. In Gavela, the world price of rice is below the domestic autarky price. A tariff is imposed but the country is too small to affect the world price.

Answer parts (a)–(c) using the initial scenario. For part (d) only, consider the following additional evidence, which may change an initial assumption.

Additional application evidence: Foreign suppliers absorb part of the tariff in their margins.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define a tariff.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using a diagram, explain its effects on domestic production, consumption and imports.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain a likely consumer cost and government benefit.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how the additional evidence changes or qualifies the economic interpretation in this case.

steps.text: A tax on imported goods or services.
It raises the domestic import price relative to the untaxed world price, assuming pass-through in the small-country model.
Label domestic S and D, world price and world price+tariff.
Show production rising, consumption falling and the import gap narrowing.
Domestic producers expand along supply at the higher price.
Consumers contract quantity demanded; imports equal the remaining gap.
Consumers pay more and lose consumer surplus.
Government receives revenue on imports that still enter; the revenue is a transfer rather than the entire welfare effect.
Identify the economic determinant, constraint or model assumption affected by this evidence, distinguishing it from the conditions used in the initial analysis.
Full pass-through is no longer assured; the domestic price increase can be less than the tariff. A justified causal link is required for this explanation mark.

subject: economics
title: Import quotas and licence rents — Jorven
stem:
All places and values are fictional. In Jorven, an import quota limits the quantity of furniture below the free-trade import level. Private firms hold the import licences without paying an auction fee.

Answer parts (a)–(c) using the initial scenario. For part (d) only, consider the following additional evidence, which may change an initial assumption.

Additional application evidence: Licences are auctioned competitively by government.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define an import quota.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the domestic price tends to rise.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a quota need not provide the same government revenue as a tariff.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how the additional evidence changes or qualifies the economic interpretation in this case.

steps.text: A quantitative restriction on imports over a period.
A binding quota permits less than the otherwise desired import volume.
The import restriction reduces available foreign supply.
At the old price, domestic demand exceeds domestic supply plus permitted imports.
The domestic price rises until that gap equals the quota.
Licence holders may buy at the world price and sell at the higher domestic price.
They capture quota rents if licences are allocated free.
Government obtains those rents only if it charges/auctions licences or otherwise collects revenue; a quota alone is not a tax.
Identify the economic determinant, constraint or model assumption affected by this evidence, distinguishing it from the conditions used in the initial analysis.
Government may capture quota rents; the original free-licence revenue conclusion changes. A justified causal link is required for this explanation mark.

stem:
This is a fictional small-country case in Arden. Inverse demand P=120−Q and domestic inverse supply P=20+Q, with P in crowns/unit and Q in units/day. World price is 40 crowns and a proposed tariff is 10 crowns/unit. The country cannot influence world price; no externalities are assumed for the calculations. Some workers in the import-competing industry have few alternative local jobs.

This full Paper 3 style case awards 20 analytic marks and 10 policy marks. Show working; use exact values or two decimal places and retain units.

Implementation evidence: Implementation can be phased and audited before nationwide expansion.

title: Specialization, trade and adjustment — Elarin
stem:
All outputs are constructed. Home and Partner each have linear PPCs. Maximum outputs using all resources are shown below.

| Economy | Food units/day | Cloth units/day |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Home | 80 | 40 |
| Partner | 60 | 60 |

Initially each devotes half its resources to each good. They consider full specialization by comparative advantage, then trade 10 units of cloth from Partner to Home at 1.50 food units per cloth. Workers cannot all move between sectors immediately.

This full Paper 3 style case awards 20 analytic marks and 10 policy marks. Show working; use exact values or two decimal places and retain units.

Implementation evidence: Implementation can be phased and audited before nationwide expansion.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate opportunity costs of one cloth unit and identify comparative advantage.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate combined output of each good before and after full specialization.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate Home's consumption after specialization and trade, and state whether the quantities alone establish that Home is better off.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate Partner's post-trade consumption and explain the terms-of-trade condition.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Explain two limitations of applying this model directly to policy.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recommend a trade and adjustment strategy, using the production and consumption calculations.

steps.text: Home:2 food units per cloth.
Partner:1 food unit per cloth.
Partner has comparative advantage in cloth.

Initial cloth=50 units/day.
Specialized food=80 units/day.
Specialized cloth=60 units/day.
Food exported=1.50×10=15.
Home food=65 units/day.
Home cloth=10 units/day.
This allocation need not give Home more of both goods than its initial bundle; whether Home prefers it depends on preferences, so these quantities alone do not establish higher welfare.
Partner food=15 units/day.
Partner cloth=50 units/day.
The 1.50-food rate lies between the 1 and 2-food opportunity costs.
It offers potential exchange gains relative to producing the imported good domestically; actual distribution and preferences still matter.
The model assumes constant opportunity costs and smooth resource reallocation.
Immobile workers can experience adjustment unemployment.
Transport costs, trade barriers and changing technology are omitted.
These can reduce or redistribute the predicted gains and change comparative advantage.

stem:

stem:

A water project costs 60000 crowns and a training programme costs 40000 crowns. The annual available budget is 220000 crowns. A survey counts 400 adults in the labour force and 40 unemployed.
